series_manifest.label: Interest Paid on National Debt (Annual Rate)

events.label: Pandemic spending peaks at $7.6 trillion a year
Interest on the debt passes $1 trillion a year

explanation.summary: The federal government's debt, its tax revenue, its total spending, and the interest it pays on the debt. When spending is above revenue, the gap is borrowed and the debt grows. Interest on that debt is now one of the largest items in the budget.
explanation.methodology: Total public debt from the Treasury via FRED (GFDEBTN, quarterly). Revenue and spending are 12-month running totals of the Monthly Treasury Statement (FRED MTSR133FMS and MTSO133FMS). Interest payments are BEA federal interest payments at an annual rate (A091RC1Q027SBEA). The split between mandatory and discretionary spending is only published yearly, so total spending is shown.

key_findings.title: 1998: A Budget Surplus
key_findings.description: Over 12 months the government collected $1.73 trillion and spent $1.65 trillion. Revenue was higher than spending.
key_findings.significance: The last time the US ran a surplus.

key_findings.title: 2021: Pandemic Spending Peak
key_findings.description: Spending over 12 months reached $7.6 trillion, the highest on the chart, as relief programs paid out.
key_findings.significance: Emergency spending added trillions to the debt in two years.

key_findings.title: Late 2023: Interest Passes $1 Trillion
key_findings.description: Interest payments passed $1 trillion a year. As of 2026, debt is $39.5 trillion, interest is about $1.28 trillion a year, and spending ($7.1 trillion) is about $1.7 trillion more than revenue ($5.4 trillion).
key_findings.significance: The more the government owes, and the higher interest rates are (see chart 4), the more interest it pays.
